The first day of the audit
Monday, 15 November 2032, nine o’clock sharp. Bertrand Vidal, a magistrate at the Court of Audit, arrives at the network’s office in Croix-Rousse for a three-week audit. Amina is waiting for him.
Mrs Diallo? Bertrand Vidal, Court of Audit. You were informed of my visit, I believe.
Yes, sir. Everything has been prepared. An office has been reserved for you at the end of the corridor.
Thank you. To begin with, I’d like to know how the subsidies are paid to the network.
They are paid by the ministry twice a year. Each payment is recorded in this spreadsheet.
And the expenses? Who are they authorised by?
Any expense over five hundred euros must be signed by Mr Moreau and by me. It’s never done any other way.
All of them. They have been scanned, filed and numbered. You’ll find them on this USB stick.
(leafing through the binder) I had been told you were organised. I hadn’t been told how organised.
It was decided from the start that everything would be transparent. It’s public money.
That’s rare, madam. Believe me, it’s very rare.
Your coffee will be ready in five minutes. Black, no sugar?

1. The passive: être + participle, in all tenses
The passive is formed with “être” in the required tense + the past participle, which AGREES with the subject:
In the passé composé passive there are TWO participles: “a été” (invariable) + the verb’s participle (agreeing): “Elles ont été scannées.”
Usually the doer of the action is introduced by “par”. But with verbs of feeling and state, “de” is used:
La salle a été construite par Radu.
La dépense est signée par Amina.
Il est respecté de ses collègues.
Le violon a été réparé par le luthier.
La table était couverte de papiers.
Le ruban a été coupé par Madame Faure.
Verbs that usually take “de”: aimer, détester, respecter, connaître, craindre, couvrir, entourer, remplir, accompagner (sometimes “par” as well).
3. Avoiding the passive: “on” and the pronominal passive
Spoken French uses the passive less than written Romanian. Two very common alternatives:
I had been told you were organised. (on = someone)
It’s never done any other way. (pronominal passive)
The pronominal passive often describes a habit or a general rule: “Ça ne se dit pas.” = That isn’t said. “Ça se voit.” = It shows.
4. The trap: verbs with an indirect object
Only the DIRECT object can become the subject of a passive. Verbs built with “à” (demander à, dire à, permettre à, promettre à) have no ordinary passive:
Il a été dit la vérité.
On lui a dit la vérité.
Elle a été permis de partir.
On lui a permis de partir. / Elle s’est vu permettre de partir.
In Romanian we say “Mi s-a cerut să vin”, but in French you CANNOT make “moi” the subject. Use “on” or “se voir” (chapter 77).
In official texts (reports, minutes, decisions), the impersonal passive with “il” is very common:
It was decided to extend the audit.
It is recommended that these methods be circulated. (+ subjunctive)
“Il est recommandé / demandé / souhaitable que” take the subjunctive. “Il a été constaté / décidé / établi que” take the indicative.
Je me suis demandé de venir.
The hall will be opened in January.

The letter arrived on Monday 8 November 2032, in a thick envelope bearing the logo of the Court of Audit. Julien opened it at the Croix-Rousse office, standing up, taking off his coat. He read it once, then a second time, turning pale. The “Musique en partage” network had been selected for an in-depth audit of its management. A magistrate would be sent on site the following week, for three weeks.

Julien handed the letter to Amina without a word. Amina read it in silence, without changing expression. Then something happened that nobody at the office had seen in five years. Amina smiled. Not a small polite smile. A real smile, broad, almost greedy, like a chess player who finally sees the opponent she has been waiting for for years.

“Let them come,” she said. Then she opened her computer, created a new folder called “Court of Audit”, and copied into it, in ten minutes, two hundred and fourteen spreadsheets. Every euro received by the network since 2028 was recorded there. Every euro spent was accounted for. Every invoice had been scanned, filed, numbered. Julien watched the screen scroll. He realised he had never really known who he was working with.

Julien, for his part, stopped sleeping. In the week before the audit he woke at three in the morning, convinced he had forgotten an invoice, lost a receipt, signed something without reading it. Ioana found him one night in the kitchen, rereading bank statements from 2029. She took the papers out of his hands. “You work with Amina,” she reminded him. “Go to bed.”

The magistrate arrived on Monday 15 November at nine o’clock precisely. His name was Bertrand Vidal. He was a man of about fifty, slim, grey from head to toe: grey suit, grey tie, grey hair, grey leather briefcase. He spoke little, in a low voice, choosing each word the way you choose a tool. He shook Julien’s hand, then Amina’s, and asked for an office, a chair and silence.

He was given the small meeting room at the back, the one overlooking the courtyard. Amina handed him a USB stick containing the two hundred and fourteen spreadsheets, as well as a forty-page binder explaining how they were organised. Mr Vidal looked at the binder. He looked at the stick. He looked at Amina. Then he said, in his low voice: “In twenty-two years of my career, madam, this is the first time I’ve been handed a user manual.”

For three weeks, Mr Vidal worked in the small room, door closed, from nine to seven. He only came out to ask questions, always precise, always polite, always to Amina. How had such-and-such a subsidy been paid? By whom had such-and-such an expense been authorised? Why had such-and-such a purchase been made in Toulouse rather than in Lyon? Amina answered in under thirty seconds, opening the right spreadsheet.

After a week, a strange relationship had formed between them. They hardly spoke, but they understood each other. Mr Vidal arrived at nine; Amina had already made him a black coffee without sugar. At noon he ate a sandwich in the small room; Amina ate hers at her desk. The other staff nicknamed them “the two spreadsheets”. Neither of them seemed to find it funny.

On Wednesday 24 November, Mr Vidal came out of the small room with a sheet of paper in his hand and a slight frown. He had found something. In the instrument repairs spreadsheet, one line intrigued him. Forty-three instruments, sent to Mirecourt, repaired by a certain Gérard Thiébaut. Total cost to the network: zero euros. “That isn’t done, madam,” he said. “Nobody repairs forty-three instruments for free.”

Amina opened another spreadsheet. It contained the dates of dispatch, the dates of return, photos of each instrument before and after repair, and a copy of Gérard Thiébaut’s letter offering his services. Mr Vidal read everything. Then he said he had to check on site. It was the procedure. A free service could hide a conflict of interest. He would leave for Mirecourt the next morning.

Mirecourt is a small town in the Vosges, grey and quiet, with a river running through it. Violins have been made there since the seventeenth century. There are workshops in almost every street, a museum of violin-making, and a school people come to from all over the world to learn the trade. Mr Vidal arrived on Thursday late in the morning, in a fine rain. He found Gérard Thiébaut’s workshop at the back of a cobbled courtyard.

The workshop smelled of wood, glue and varnish. Violins hung from the ceiling like hams in a farmhouse. On the workbench, an open double bass waited, its belly empty. Gérard Thiébaut, eighty since August, wore a leather apron and glasses on the end of his nose. He looked at Mr Vidal’s grey suit, his grey briefcase, his grey umbrella. Then he said: “You’ve come to inspect me. Come in, it’s raining.”

Mr Vidal asked his questions. Gérard Thiébaut answered them while carrying on working. No, he wasn’t paid. No, he had no connection with the network, or with the Moreau family. No, he received no benefit. The materials? He paid for them himself, out of his pension. Why? Gérard Thiébaut put down his tool. He took off his glasses. He looked Mr Vidal straight in the eye for the first time.

“Because in sixty years in the trade,” he said, “I’ve repaired violins for soloists, national orchestras, Japanese collectors. Instruments worth the price of a house. And they were played three times a year, in halls where seats cost a hundred euros. These ones are played every day. By children who would never have touched a violin otherwise. Do you understand the difference?”

Then he took a small folded piece of paper, a little crumpled, out of a drawer. It was the note Yanis had slipped into his cello case in the spring: “Sir, take care of him. He has a difficult character, but he sings well.” Gérard Thiébaut had kept it. He kept it in the drawer where he stored his most precious tools. Mr Vidal read the note. He didn’t put it in his report.

Then the luthier showed him round the violin-making school at the end of the street. In a big, bright workshop, about twenty apprentices from all over the world were working in silence: a Japanese woman, two Koreans, a Brazilian, a young woman from Marseille. Each was making their first violin, which would be finished in three years. “Here,” said Gérard Thiébaut, “we don’t count in hours. We count in years.” Mr Vidal wrote the sentence in his grey notebook.

Before he left, Gérard Thiébaut did something strange. He took a violin down from the ceiling, an old brown violin, very plain, and handed it to the inspector with a bow. “Play me something,” he said. “You have a violinist’s hands. I saw it straight away.” Mr Vidal wanted to refuse. Then, slowly, as if in spite of himself, he took the violin and tucked it under his chin.

He had played the violin from the age of six to fourteen. He was gifted. His teacher wanted to enrol him at the Nancy Conservatoire. But his father, an accountant at a shoe factory, had said music didn’t feed a man, and the violin had been sold the year he turned fourteen. He had never touched one again. He had studied law, then public finance. He had never told anyone.

He played a few notes, clumsy, out of tune. Then his fingers remembered. He played the opening of a sonatina he had been working on at thirteen and had never been able to finish. Gérard Thiébaut listened without a word, arms folded. When Mr Vidal stopped, there were tears on his grey cheeks. The luthier handed him a varnish-stained handkerchief. “It’s yours,” he said. “The violin. Not the handkerchief.”

Mr Vidal refused, of course. A magistrate of the Court of Audit could accept no gift from a person under inspection. It was forbidden. So he insisted on buying it, at market price, with a proper receipt. Gérard Thiébaut sighed, set a ridiculously low price, and wrote a receipt by hand on a scrap of manuscript paper. Mr Vidal left in the rain, a violin case in one hand and his grey briefcase in the other.

That evening, in his hotel room in Lyon, he opened the case. He tuned the violin slowly, listening hard. Then he played, very softly, the unfinished sonatina. After ten minutes there was a knock on the partition wall. He stopped dead, embarrassed. An old lady’s voice on the other side of the wall said: “No, no, carry on! It’s the first time in years anyone has given me a concert.” He carried on.

Back in Lyon, he said nothing about his trip. He simply wrote in his report that Mr Thiébaut’s service had been checked on site and that no conflict of interest had been found. But Amina, who noticed everything, noticed the violin case standing in a corner of the small meeting room. She asked no questions. She just added, the next day, a second sugar lump next to his coffee. He put it in his cup.

In the second week, Mr Vidal asked to see an orchestra. Not figures: children. It was unusual, but not forbidden. Julien took him to La Duchère one Wednesday afternoon. Théo was rehearsing a new Christmas piece with the sixty children. The inspector sat at the back of the Salle Hélène Morel, on a plastic chair, his notebook on his knees. He wrote nothing for two hours.

He watched Yanis, thirteen now, tune his red cello, repaired in Mirecourt. He watched Sami, who hardly ever spoke, play a flute solo with his eyes closed. He watched a little girl of eight, who had arrived in September, holding her first violin like a wounded bird. During the break he went over to her. Without a word, he showed her how to place her thumb on the bow. She tried. The sound became clearer.

Théo, who had seen everything, came over in turn. He asked the inspector whether he played. Mr Vidal hesitated for a long time. Then he answered: “I used to play. A long time ago. And for the past week, I’ve been playing a little again. In the evenings, at the hotel. Softly, so as not to disturb the neighbours.” Théo asked nothing more. He simply told him the hall was open every Wednesday and there was always a free chair.

The audit ended on Friday 3 December. Mr Vidal called Julien and Amina into the small room for the closing meeting. In front of him he had a twenty-page file, his notes, and a single separate sheet. He started with the separate sheet. “I have found an irregularity,” he announced in his low voice. Amina went white. Julien felt his heart stop.

The irregularity concerned a sum of forty-seven euros and twenty cents. An invoice from a garden centre in Villeurbanne, dated October 2030: a bag of potting compost and a wooden stake, bought for planting the La Duchère lime tree. The expense had been filed under “Musical equipment” instead of “Outdoor improvements”. A filing error. The only one, in two hundred and fourteen spreadsheets and four years of accounts.

Amina was devastated. She said it was entirely her fault, that she would repay the forty-seven euros twenty out of her own pocket, that she apologised to the network, to the Court of Audit and to the Republic. Mr Vidal let her finish. Then he said, with something resembling a smile: “Madam, I have audited entire ministries where millions had been lost. This isn’t an irregularity. It’s a signature.”

He added that a lime tree could, after all, probably be considered musical equipment, since music was played under its branches. He would record it as an inconsequential allocation error, corrected on site. Then he opened the twenty-page file and read its conclusion aloud. Julien listened without breathing. Amina looked at the window, her hands clenched on her knees.

“It was found that the public funds allocated to the network have been used in a rigorous, transparent manner in keeping with their purpose. The network’s management may be described as exemplary. It is recommended that the financial monitoring methods introduced by Mrs Amina Diallo be studied and shared with other state cultural programmes.” Mr Vidal closed the file.

There was a long silence. Then Amina stood up. She said “Excuse me” in a choked voice, left the small room, crossed the office, went into her own office and closed the door. For the third time since Julien had known her. Through the door, he heard her crying for a long time. Mr Vidal packed up his things without a word. He left his card on the table.

On the back of the card he had written, in his fine grey handwriting: “For Mrs Diallo, from a colleague.” Amina found it when she came out of her office an hour later, her eyes red. She read it. She turned it over. Then she opened her computer, created a new spreadsheet called “Colleagues”, and entered a single name in it. She saved the file twice. To be safe.

December went by very quickly. The orchestras were preparing their Christmas concerts. The eight building sites were progressing despite the cold. In Brest, the old fish market had received its big skylight. In Metz, the foundations had been poured. And in Grenoble, the hall was finished. The opening had been set for Saturday 15 January 2033. The invitations had been sent. Mrs Faure had agreed to cut the ribbon.

On 23 December, for what would have been Odile’s eighty-second birthday, the family gathered at Isabelle’s, as the year before. But this time there was one more baby. Little Yves, seven months old, was placed in Odile’s armchair between two cushions, like a king on his throne. He looked at everyone very seriously. Then he grabbed the blue shawl and put it in his mouth.

Yves Le Goff had come from Nantes, as promised. He had brought his pan, of course, but also a surprise: a small wooden box containing a miniature copper sextant, which he had had made for his godson by a craftsman in Saint-Malo. “We’ll teach him to use it when he can count to ten,” he announced. Little Yves tried to eat the sextant. He was judged too young for navigation.

Inès had come too, with an unexpected guest: Clémence, the minister’s daughter, who was spending the Christmas holidays at her home in La Duchère. The two girls had been writing to each other every day since the Odéon. The minister had hesitated at first, then let his daughter go, on condition that she called him every evening. After dinner, the violinist and the clarinettist played a duet they had composed together, by text message, all autumn.

The duet was called “The Landing”. It began with three notes on the clarinet, to which the violin answered with three others, then the two instruments chased each other, lost each other, found each other again, like two neighbours talking from one door to the other. In the middle there was a silence of eight bars. Isabelle listened with her eyes closed. At the end she asked if she could have the score. She wanted to frame it.

That evening, Julien told the story of the inspector and the violin. He only knew half of it, the half Théo had told him, but he told it well. Isabelle laughed. Yves said accountants were like sailors: they all had a song hidden away somewhere that they only sang once in their lives. Rose-Hélène asked what an inspector was. It was explained to her. She thought it was a sad job.

“Not necessarily,” said Julien. “This one was looking for mistakes. And he found something he had lost.” Rose-Hélène thought about it. She asked what thing. Julien answered: a violin. Rose-Hélène thought that was a very good thing to find again, and that the inspector had been lucky. Then she played the three notes, for Odile, as every year. And everyone whistled the rest.

On Saturday 15 January 2033, Grenoble woke up under a perfectly blue sky. It had snowed in the night. The peaks shone all around the city like a crown. In front of the old glove factory, on rue des Tanneurs, a crowd had gathered from nine o’clock: neighbourhood residents, parents, children from the nearby school, councillors, journalists, and all Joseph’s carpenters, wearing suits for the first time in their lives.

On the brick façade, a plaque had been put up the day before, still hidden under a white sheet. Radu had had it engraved in Lyon, in secret. Nobody knew what was written on it except him, Joseph and Mrs Rey. Mrs Rey was sitting in the front row, on her chair, wrapped in three scarves, her cane between her knees. She was eighty-three. She had been there since eight. She didn’t want to miss this.

Mrs Faure spoke first, as always. But this time her speech lasted three minutes, and it ended with a sentence nobody expected: “I had said I would not oppose it, provided the roof held. The roof holds. I was wrong about the rest.” Then she cut the ribbon, to applause, with a pair of scissors lent to her by Mathis.

Then Joseph pulled the white sheet. The plaque appeared, copper, gleaming in the winter sun. It read: “Salle des Gantières. Here, from 1891 to 1995, women sewed gloves for hands they would never see. From now on, children play music here with their own.” Mrs Rey read the plaque. She took a handkerchief out of one of her three scarves. She said nothing.

Inside, the hall was flooded with light. The sun came in through the big skylight and fell like a column in the middle of the hall, on the forty children of Grenoble’s new orchestra, seated in a semicircle with their brand-new instruments. At the back, behind a red drum kit donated by the carpenters, Mathis was waiting, sticks raised, as serious as a conductor. Théo had come from Lyon to conduct the first concert.

In the crowd, in the third row, there was a woman of about forty standing very straight, a little apart. Joseph recognised her and discreetly pointed her out to Julien. It was Mathis’s former teacher, the one who used to punish him every week for drumming on the tables. She had come of her own accord. When Mathis saw her, he hesitated for a second. Then he gave her a little wave with his drumstick.

They played Henri’s waltz. Of course. All the network’s new halls began with it. The forty children had rehearsed it all autumn under a young Grenoble teacher, and they played it their own way, a little too fast, with a drum kit that didn’t exist in Henri’s version. But nobody complained. Mrs Rey beat time with her cane.

At the third verse, at the moment of silence, the forty children stopped together. Mathis too, his sticks suspended in mid-air. Eight bars. Rose-Hélène, sitting on Julien’s knees in the second row, took a breath to whistle. But before she could, someone at the back of the hall played the three notes. Not on a harmonica. On a violin. A slightly hesitant, slightly rusty sound, but in tune.

The whole hall turned round. Standing against the back wall, in his grey suit, an old brown violin under his chin, was Bertrand Vidal. Nobody had seen him come in. He hadn’t been invited. He had read the announcement of the opening in the paper, and had taken the six a.m. train from Paris with his Mirecourt violin. He lowered his bow, bright red, like a child caught misbehaving.

There was a moment of astonishment. Then Rose-Hélène, who had never seen this man in her life, did what she always did. She answered. She whistled the next three notes, off-key, with lots of air, as hard as she could. Mr Vidal looked at her. He smiled. A real smile this time, without any hesitation. Then he raised his violin again and played the rest, to the end of the silence.

Mathis struck the first beat of the reprise. The orchestra set off again. And for the whole end of the waltz, the inspector from the Court of Audit played with the forty children of Grenoble, standing against the back wall, eyes closed, as if catching up in a few minutes on thirty-six years of silence. In the front row, Amina, whom Julien had invited, watched him without moving, her hands clenched on her bag.

After the concert he wanted to leave discreetly. Amina caught up with him on the pavement, in the snow. They looked at each other for a moment, two grey, precise people in the middle of a laughing crowd. Then Amina said that an orchestra for adult beginners was going to be set up in Lyon in the spring, on Thursday evenings. She had already made the registration spreadsheet. There was one violin place left.

Mr Vidal thought about it. He said he lived in Paris. That he worked a lot. That it probably wasn’t reasonable. Amina replied that she had checked the train times: there was one every hour, and the journey took two hours. She had made a spreadsheet. Mr Vidal looked at her for a long time. Then he took a small grey notebook out of his pocket and wrote, very carefully: “Thursday. Lyon. Violin.”

On the train, Julien reread the report’s conclusion one last time, printed and folded in his jacket pocket. “It was found that the public funds have been used in a rigorous manner.” He knew the sentence by heart. He thought of Odile, who used to say emotions were facts too. And he told himself that, for once, an official report had managed to record both at the same time.

That evening, on the train home, Julien asked Amina whether she was really going to set up an adult orchestra in the spring. Amina looked out of the window at the mountains disappearing into the night. Then she admitted that no. That project didn’t exist. Not yet. But she had just drawn up its budget in her head, and it was perfectly balanced. Julien burst out laughing. Amina, for the second time in her life, smiled in front of him.

An extract from Mr Vidal’s report on the “Musique en partage” network. Administrative texts make heavy use of the passive and the impersonal passive. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Rapport de contrôle : réseau « Musique en partage »
The audit was carried out from 15 November to 3 December 2032 at the network’s premises in Lyon. It was supplemented by an on-site visit to Mirecourt and by observing a rehearsal at La Duchère.

Since 2028, the network has been funded mainly by the Ministry of Culture. The subsidies are paid twice a year. They have been used entirely for the planned activities: teachers’ salaries, purchase and maintenance of instruments, rental and renovation of halls.
Each expense has been checked. All invoices have been kept and are accessible in digital form. Expenses above five hundred euros are systematically authorised by two signatories.
A single error was noted: an expense of 47.20 euros, linked to the planting of a tree, was filed in an inappropriate category. This error was corrected on site. It has no consequences.
The free repair of forty-three instruments by a volunteer luthier has been verified. No conflict of interest was found.
In conclusion, it was found that public funds have been used in a rigorous and transparent manner. It is recommended that the network’s monitoring methods be studied by other state programmes.
